translations.idiomatic: I compose this poem to voice my grief; leaning on the chariot rail, tears soak my cap-strings.

translations.literal: Section Five
translations.idiomatic: Fifth section

translations.literal: "Morning Sun" / "How Excellent" — text by Emperor Wen of Wei,
translations.idiomatic: "Morning Sun" (tune: "How Excellent") — text by Emperor Wen of Wei,

translations.literal: Section Five
translations.idiomatic: Fifth section

sentences.zh: 朝日樂相樂，酣飲不知醉。

translations.literal: At morning sun, joy upon joy; we drink deep and know not drunkenness.
translations.idiomatic: In the morning sun we rejoice together; we drink deep and never feel drunk.

sentences.zh: 悲弦激新聲，長笛吐清氣。

translations.literal: Grieving strings stir new sounds; the long flute breathes clear tone.
translations.idiomatic: Mournful strings strike up fresh melodies; the long flute pours out pure breath.

translations.literal: Section One
translations.idiomatic: First section

sentences.zh: 弦歌感人腸，四坐皆歡說。

translations.literal: String and song touch the human heart; all four sides of the hall rejoice.
translations.idiomatic: Strings and song move the heart; everyone in the hall rejoices.

sentences.zh: 寥寥高堂上，涼風入我室。

translations.literal: In the lofty hall, vast and still; cool breeze enters my chamber.
translations.idiomatic: In the lofty, empty hall, a cool breeze enters my room.

translations.literal: Section Two
translations.idiomatic: Second section

sentences.zh: 持滿如不盈，有得者能卒。

translations.literal: Hold fullness as if not overflowing; those who gain can see it through to the end.
translations.idiomatic: Hold fullness as though the cup were not full; those who attain can carry it through.

sentences.zh: 君子多苦心，所愁不但一。

translations.literal: The noble person bears much bitter care; what he grieves is never only one thing.
translations.idiomatic: The gentleman toils at heart; his worries are never just one.

translations.literal: Section Three
translations.idiomatic: Third section

sentences.zh: 慊慊下白屋，吐握不可失。

translations.literal: Eagerly he descends to humble thatched cottages; spitting out food and clasping hands—he must not fail.
translations.idiomatic: Humbly he visits poor thatched cottages; like the Duke of Zhou, he never neglects to receive guests.

sentences.zh: 眾賓飽滿歸，主人苦不悉。

translations.literal: All the guests leave replete; the host still grieves he has not done enough.
translations.idiomatic: Every guest departs full and satisfied, yet the host still frets he has not done enough.

translations.literal: Section Four
translations.idiomatic: Fourth section

sentences.zh: 比翼翔雲漢，羅者安所羈。

translations.literal: Wings joined, they soar through cloud and Milky Way; where could the netter hold them?
translations.idiomatic: Wing to wing they fly through cloud and sky; what fowler could ever snare them?

sentences.zh: 沖靜得自然，榮華何足為。

translations.literal: In emptiness and stillness one attains the natural; what need is there for glory and splendor?
translations.idiomatic: In quiet emptiness one finds the natural way; what need is there for pomp and glory?

translations.literal: Section Five
translations.idiomatic: Fifth section

translations.literal: "Up the Mountain" / "How Excellent" — text by Emperor Wen of Wei
translations.idiomatic: "Up the Mountain" (tune: "How Excellent") — text by Emperor Wen of Wei

translations.literal: Section Six
translations.idiomatic: Sixth section

translations.literal: Up the mountain to gather ferns; at dusk, bitter hunger.
translations.idiomatic: I climb the mountain to gather ferns; at dusk I suffer bitter hunger.

translations.literal: In stream valleys winds blow often; frost and dew soak my clothes.
translations.idiomatic: Wind blows often in the valleys; frost and dew drench my clothes.

translations.literal: Section One
translations.idiomatic: First section

translations.literal: Wild pheasants call in flock; gibbons and macaques chase one another.
translations.idiomatic: Wild pheasants cry in flocks; apes and gibbons chase each other.

translations.literal: Turning back I gaze toward home—how layered, how heaped with grief,
translations.idiomatic: I turn and look toward home—how thickly grief piles up,

translations.literal: Section Two
translations.idiomatic: Second section

translations.literal: High mountains have their cliffs; forest trees have their branches.
translations.idiomatic: Lofty peaks have their escarpments; trees in the woods have their boughs.

translations.literal: Grief comes from nowhere; no one knows it.
translations.idiomatic: Sorrow arrives from no direction; no one can fathom it.

translations.literal: Section Three
translations.idiomatic: Third section

translations.literal: Human life is like lodging—what use so many cares?
translations.idiomatic: Life is but a brief stay—why heap up so many worries?

translations.literal: Now that I find no joy, the years race on.
translations.idiomatic: If I take no joy today, the years will gallop past.

translations.literal: Section Four
translations.idiomatic: Fourth section

translations.literal: Surging, surging flows the river; midstream a boat goes by.
translations.idiomatic: The river rolls on and on; a boat travels midstream.

translations.literal: Tossed on the waves, drifting thin—much like a traveler's wanderings.
translations.idiomatic: Carried on the waves, tossed and thinned—like a wanderer far from home.

translations.literal: Section Five
translations.idiomatic: Fifth section

translations.literal: I whip my fine horse; I wrap myself in light fur.
translations.idiomatic: I spur my good horse and wrap myself in a light fur coat.

translations.literal: Now galloping, now racing—just to forget my grief awhile.
translations.idiomatic: Now flying, now driving on—to ease my sorrow for a while.

translations.literal: Section Six
translations.idiomatic: Sixth section

translations.literal: "Morning Wander" / "How Excellent" — text by Emperor Wen of Wei
translations.idiomatic: "Morning Wander" (tune: "How Excellent") — text by Emperor Wen of Wei

translations.literal: Section Five
translations.idiomatic: Fifth section

sentences.zh: 朝遊高臺觀，夕宴華池陰。

translations.literal: Morning roaming at the high terrace hall; evening feast in shade of the splendid pool.
translations.idiomatic: In the morning I roam the high terrace; in the evening I feast in the shade of the splendid pool.

sentences.zh: 大酋奉甘醪，狩人獻嘉禽。

translations.literal: The master of feasts offers sweet wine; huntsmen present fine fowl.
translations.idiomatic: The feast-master serves sweet liquor; hunters bring fine game birds.

translations.literal: Section One
translations.idiomatic: First section

sentences.zh: 齊倡發東舞，秦箏奏西音。

translations.literal: Qi singers lead eastern dance; Qin zithers play western melodies.
translations.idiomatic: Qi performers lead dances from the east; Qin zithers sound melodies from the west.

sentences.zh: 有客從南來，為我彈清琴。

translations.literal: A guest comes from the south to pluck the clear qin for me.
translations.idiomatic: A guest arrives from the south and plays the clear-toned qin for me.

translations.literal: Section Two
translations.idiomatic: Second section

sentences.zh: 五音紛繁會，拊者激微吟。

translations.literal: Five tones mingle in profusion; the striker stirs subtle humming song.
translations.idiomatic: The five tones weave together richly; the player strikes up a subtle hum.

sentences.zh: 淫魚乘波聽，踴躍自浮沉。

translations.literal: Deep-water fish listen riding the waves; leaping, they sink and rise of themselves.
translations.idiomatic: Fish in the deep listen as they ride the waves, leaping and diving of their own accord.

translations.literal: Section Three
translations.idiomatic: Third section

sentences.zh: 飛鳥翻翔舞，悲鳴集北林。

translations.literal: Flying birds wheel and dance in air; mournful cries gather in the north grove.
translations.idiomatic: Birds wheel and dance in flight; sad cries gather in the northern woods.

sentences.zh: 樂極哀情來，憀亮摧肝心。

translations.literal: When joy reaches its limit, sorrow comes; desolate and bright, it shatters heart and liver.
translations.idiomatic: When pleasure peaks, grief arrives; bleak and piercing, it wrecks the heart.

translations.literal: Section Four
translations.idiomatic: Fourth section

sentences.zh: 清角豈不妙，德薄所不任。

translations.literal: How could the clear jue mode not be exquisite? My virtue is too thin to bear it.
translations.idiomatic: Is not the clear jue mode wondrous? My virtue is too slight to sustain it.

sentences.zh: 大哉子野言，弭弦且自禁。

translations.literal: Great are Master Ye's words—I still the strings and restrain myself.
translations.idiomatic: How great Master Ye's saying is—I slacken the strings and hold myself back.

translations.literal: Section Five
translations.idiomatic: Fifth section

translations.literal: "Lord Ancient" / "How Excellent" — text by Emperor Wu of Wei,
translations.idiomatic: "Lord Ancient" (tune: "How Excellent") — text by Emperor Wu of Wei,

translations.literal: Section Seven
translations.idiomatic: Seventh section

translations.literal: Lord Ancient Danfu—accumulating virtue, handing down benevolence.
translations.idiomatic: Old Lord Danfu piled up virtue and bequeathed benevolence.

translations.literal: He thought to spread the Way; a sage king at Bin.
translations.idiomatic: He sought to enlarge the Way—a sage king at Bin.

translations.literal: Section One
translations.idiomatic: First section

translations.literal: Taibo and Zhongyong—regal virtue and benevolence.
translations.idiomatic: Taibo and Zhongyong embodied royal virtue and humaneness.

translations.literal: Their deeds lasted a hundred generations; they cut their hair and tattooed their bodies.
translations.idiomatic: Their influence ran a hundred generations; they cropped their hair and tattooed their bodies.

translations.literal: Section Two
translations.idiomatic: Second section

translations.literal: Boyi and Shuqi—worthies left from antiquity.
translations.idiomatic: Boyi and Shuqi—sages bequeathed from olden times.

translations.literal: They yielded the realm and were not employed; they starved to death on Mount Shou.
translations.idiomatic: They declined the state and would not serve; they starved on Mount Shou.

translations.literal: Section Three
translations.idiomatic: Third section

translations.literal: How wise was Shanfu, minister to that King Xuan!
translations.idiomatic: How wise was Shanfu, who assisted King Xuan!

translations.literal: Why employ Duke Du and burden our sage and worthy men?
translations.idiomatic: Why use Duke Du and weigh down our sages and worthies?

translations.literal: Section Four
translations.idiomatic: Fourth section

translations.literal: Duke Huan of Qi's hegemony relied on getting Zhongfu.
translations.idiomatic: Duke Huan of Qi's dominance depended on winning Zhongfu.

translations.literal: Later he entrusted Shu Diao—and worms crawled out the door.
translations.idiomatic: Later he trusted Shu Diao—and maggots crawled out the door.

translations.literal: Section Five
translations.idiomatic: Fifth section

translations.literal: Yanzi Pingzhong—he piled up virtue together with benevolence.
translations.idiomatic: Yanzi Pingzhong amassed virtue and humaneness alike.

translations.literal: He sank his virtue into the age; he need not have brooded on fate.
translations.idiomatic: He submerged his virtue in the world; he need not have fretted over destiny.

translations.literal: Section Six
translations.idiomatic: Sixth section

translations.literal: In Confucius's age, kingdoms had their lords.
translations.idiomatic: In Confucius's time, each kingdom had its ruler.

translations.literal: Each according to rule drank wine; waves were stirred to dispatch officers.
translations.idiomatic: By their customs they drank wine; surging waves sent officers forth.

translations.literal: Section Seven
translations.idiomatic: Seventh section

translations.literal: "Cherishing Myself" / "How Excellent" — text by Emperor Wu of Wei
translations.idiomatic: "Cherishing Myself" (tune: "How Excellent") — text by Emperor Wu of Wei

translations.literal: Section Six
translations.idiomatic: Sixth section

sentences.zh: 自惜身薄祐，夙賤罹孤苦。

translations.literal: I pity myself—thin in blessed fortune; from youth lowly, I met orphan solitude.
translations.idiomatic: I grieve for myself—little blessed; born lowly, I knew orphan loneliness early.

sentences.zh: 既無三徙教，不聞過庭語。

translations.literal: I had no thrice-moved teaching; I heard no words across the courtyard.
translations.idiomatic: I never received the thrice-moved instruction; I never heard the admonitions given in the courtyard.

translations.literal: Section One
translations.idiomatic: First section

sentences.zh: 其窮如抽裂，自以思所怙。

translations.literal: My distress is like being torn apart; I think for myself on whom I might rely.
translations.idiomatic: My plight is like being ripped asunder; I ponder alone whom I might depend on.

sentences.zh: 雖懷一介志，是時其能與。

translations.literal: Though I harbor a single stalk of resolve, in that hour who could join me?
translations.idiomatic: Though I hold one stalk of loyal intent, who then could stand with me?

translations.literal: Section Two
translations.idiomatic: Second section

sentences.zh: 守窮者貧賤，惋歎淚如雨。

translations.literal: Those who keep to poverty—wretched and low—lament till tears fall like rain.
translations.idiomatic: Those who cling to poverty weep and sigh until tears fall like rain.

sentences.zh: 泣涕於悲夫，乞活安能覩。

translations.literal: Weeping before the grieving man—begging life, how can he look upon it?
translations.idiomatic: Tears before the sorrowing man—begging for life, how can he bear to see it?

translations.literal: Section Three
translations.idiomatic: Third section

sentences.zh: 我願於天窮，琅邪傾側左。

translations.literal: I wish Heaven at its extremity—Langye tilts askew to the left.
translations.idiomatic: I would that Heaven at its limit—Langye leaned and toppled leftward.

sentences.zh: 雖欲竭忠誠，欣公歸其楚。

translations.literal: Though I would exhaust loyalty, I rejoice that the lord returns to his Chu.
translations.idiomatic: Though I would spend myself in loyalty, I rejoice that my lord returns to Chu.

translations.literal: Section Four
translations.idiomatic: Fourth section

sentences.zh: 快人曰為歎，抱情不得叙。

translations.literal: A frank man speaks what is sighing; feelings held close cannot be told.
translations.idiomatic: An outspoken man calls it sighing; the feelings I hold cannot be fully spoken.

sentences.zh: 顯行天教人，誰知莫不緒。

translations.literal: Open conduct is Heaven's teaching of men—who knows? None is without thread of care.
translations.idiomatic: Open action is Heaven's way of teaching people—who understands? None is without anxious threads.

translations.literal: Section Five
translations.idiomatic: Fifth section

sentences.zh: 我願何時隨，此歎亦難處。

translations.literal: When may my wish be followed? This sigh too is hard to bear.
translations.idiomatic: When will my wish be granted? This lament too is hard to endure.

sentences.zh: 今我將何照於光燿，釋銜不如雨。

translations.literal: Now what shall I take for light and glory? Releasing the bit is not like rain.
translations.idiomatic: Now what shall I look to for brightness and honor? Letting go the bridle is not like gentle rain.

translations.literal: Section Six
translations.idiomatic: Sixth section

translations.literal: "I Depart" / "How Excellent" — text by Emperor Ming of Wei
translations.idiomatic: "I Depart" (tune: "How Excellent") — text by Emperor Ming of Wei

translations.literal: Section Eight
translations.idiomatic: Eighth section

translations.literal: I depart on campaign, to attack those barbarian captives.
translations.idiomatic: I set out on campaign to strike those savage foes.

translations.literal: We drill the army and pick the soldiers, then set our hosts in order.
translations.idiomatic: We train the troops and select the ranks, then align our columns aright.

translations.literal: Section One
translations.idiomatic: First section

translations.literal: Light boats race the river's length; first wild geese rest by the shore.
translations.idiomatic: Light craft speed along the river; early geese linger by the bank.

translations.literal: Bold and fierce, stern and resolute—like bears, like tigers.
translations.idiomatic: Stalwart and fierce, bold and steady—like bears and like tigers.

translations.literal: Section Two
translations.idiomatic: Second section

translations.literal: Beating drums like thunder; breath exhaled becomes rain.
translations.idiomatic: Drums beat like thunder; exhaled breath turns to rain.

translations.literal: Ox-tails and banners direct the host; advance and retreat answer the square.
translations.idiomatic: With pennons and banners we command; advance and retreat follow the rule.

translations.literal: Section Three
translations.idiomatic: Third section

translations.literal: A hundred horses pull even reins; the driver is like Zaofu.
translations.idiomatic: A hundred steeds match their bridles; the charioteer is Zaofu himself.

translations.literal: At ease, at ease—the six armies all share this martial might.
translations.idiomatic: Calm and orderly, the six armies all share in this prowess.

translations.literal: Section Four
translations.idiomatic: Fourth section

translations.literal: On double roads we hurry like stars; yet bright as this march is, the way is blocked.
translations.idiomatic: We rush both roads like passing stars; bright though this march is, obstacles remain.

translations.literal: Day by day we go farther; westward we leave behind Jing and Xu.
translations.idiomatic: Farther day after day; to the west we turn our backs on Jing and Xu.

translations.literal: Section Five
translations.idiomatic: Fifth section

translations.literal: The campaign does not halt ten days; we soon arrive at Yangtu.
translations.idiomatic: The march does not linger ten days; we soon reach Yangtu.

translations.literal: Fleeing rebels tremble in fear; none dare stand against our defense.
translations.idiomatic: The fleeing enemy quakes with dread; none dare meet our onslaught.

translations.literal: Section Six
translations.idiomatic: Sixth section

translations.literal: Tiger-like ministers and ranked generals—sullen anger is dispelled.
translations.idiomatic: Tiger generals and column commanders—surly wrath is smoothed away.

translations.literal: Huai and Si are cleared and quiet; we rouse Yang and drive the foe.
translations.idiomatic: The Huai and Si are pacified; we raise Yang and strike where the enemy hides.

translations.literal: Section Seven
translations.idiomatic: Seventh section

translations.literal: We deploy virtue and blaze with might—both securing and soothing.
translations.idiomatic: Virtue shines and martial glory blazes—we both hold firm and soothe the land.

translations.literal: We turn the banners homeward and report our entry to the imperial ancestor.
translations.idiomatic: We wheel the standards toward home and announce our return to the royal forebear.

translations.literal: Section Eight
translations.idiomatic: Eighth section

translations.literal: "Splendid Splendid" / "How Excellent" — text by Emperor Ming of Wei
translations.idiomatic: "Splendid Splendid" (tune: "How Excellent") — text by Emperor Ming of Wei

translations.literal: Section Four
translations.idiomatic: Fourth section

translations.literal: Splendid, splendid Great Wei—royal armies march to war.
translations.idiomatic: Glorious Great Wei—imperial forces set out on campaign.

translations.literal: Braving heat they quell rebellion; shaking and shining, martial spirit.
translations.idiomatic: Through summer heat they punish disorder; their brilliance shakes the realm.

translations.literal: Section One
translations.idiomatic: First section

translations.literal: Boats ply the Yellow River, drifting with the rippling waves.
translations.idiomatic: We float boats on the Yellow River, carried on murmuring waves.

translations.literal: Canals wind and turn; the road stretches on without end.
translations.idiomatic: Channels bend and cross; the way ahead runs on and on.

translations.literal: Section Two
translations.idiomatic: Second section

translations.literal: Feathered banners blot out the sun; pennant tassels darken the sky.
translations.idiomatic: Plumed standards hide the sun; streamers and flags shadow heaven.

translations.literal: Deep fish splash and play in the deep abyss.
translations.idiomatic: Fish in the depths splash and sport in the deep waters.

translations.literal: Section Three
translations.idiomatic: Third section

translations.literal: Only the pond and shore—follow like the stream.
translations.idiomatic: Only by pond and bank—we follow as the current flows.

translations.literal: Not acting alone, we grasp and raise Chu.
translations.idiomatic: Not alone—we hold firm and lift Yang and Chu.

translations.literal: Heart full of sorrow—I sing "Gathering Ferns."
translations.idiomatic: My heart is heavy—I sing "Gathering Ferns."

translations.literal: Heart endlessly long—there on Huai and Fei.
translations.idiomatic: Long, long my heart—there by the Huai and Fei.

translations.literal: May my lord win victory soon and return early.
translations.idiomatic: May you, my lord, prevail quickly and come home soon.

translations.literal: Section Four
translations.idiomatic: Fourth section

translations.literal: "Tomorrow" / "How Excellent" — old lyrics
translations.idiomatic: "Tomorrow" (tune: "How Excellent") — traditional lyrics

translations.literal: Section Six
translations.idiomatic: Sixth section

translations.literal: Tomorrow brings great hardship—mouth dry, lips parched.
translations.idiomatic: Tomorrow will be hard indeed—my mouth dry, my lips cracked.

translations.literal: Today let us rejoice together; all should share gladness.
translations.idiomatic: Today we feast together; let every heart be glad.

translations.literal: Section One
translations.idiomatic: First section

translations.literal: We pass famous mountains; magic fungus flutters in the wind.
translations.idiomatic: We travel famous peaks; spirit fungus waves in the breeze.

translations.literal: Immortal Wang Qiao offers a single pill of medicine.
translations.idiomatic: The immortal Wang Qiao presents one pellet of elixir.

translations.literal: Section Two
translations.idiomatic: Second section

translations.literal: I pity my short sleeves; my hands within know cold.
translations.idiomatic: My sleeves are short—I feel the cold on my bare arms.

translations.literal: Ashamed I am no Ling Zhe, to repay Lord Zhao.
translations.idiomatic: I shame myself that I am no Ling Zhe, to repay Zhao Xuan.

translations.literal: Section Three
translations.idiomatic: Third section

translations.literal: The moon sets; Shen crosses the sky; the Dipper stands athwart.
translations.idiomatic: The moon has set; Shen spans the heavens; the Northern Dipper runs crosswise.

translations.literal: Dear friends are at the door, yet hunger keeps me from eating.
translations.idiomatic: Close friends stand at the door, yet I am too hungry to eat.

translations.literal: Section Four
translations.idiomatic: Fourth section

translations.literal: Days of joy are still few; days of grief are bitter and many.
translations.idiomatic: Happy days are still few; sorrowful days are bitter and many.

translations.literal: How shall we forget care? Play zither and sing with wine.
translations.idiomatic: How forget our cares? Strum the zither and sing over wine.

translations.literal: Section Five
translations.idiomatic: Fifth section

translations.literal: The Eight Worthies of Huainan—essential Way, untroubled.
translations.idiomatic: The Eight Immortals of Huainan—the vital Way without vexation.

translations.literal: They yoke six dragons and sport among the clouds.
translations.idiomatic: They harness six dragons and roam in play above the clouds.

translations.literal: Section Six
translations.idiomatic: Sixth section

translations.literal: "East Gate" / "East Gate Ballad" — old lyrics
translations.idiomatic: "East Gate" (tune: "East Gate Ballad") — traditional lyrics

translations.literal: Section Four
translations.idiomatic: Fourth section

translations.literal: Out the east gate—I do not wish to return;
translations.idiomatic: I leave by the east gate and do not want to come back;

translations.literal: Coming in the gate, anguish— I almost weep.
translations.idiomatic: I step back inside and grief wells up—I nearly break down.

sentences.zh: 盎中無斗儲，還視桁上無縣衣。

translations.literal: No peck measure in the jar; I look back—no clothes hanging on the beam.
translations.idiomatic: The rice jar holds no peck; I look up—no robe hangs on the rafters.

translations.literal: Section One
translations.idiomatic: First section

sentences.zh: 拔劒出門去，兒女牽衣啼。

translations.literal: I draw my sword and go out the gate; my children clutch my robe and weep.
translations.idiomatic: I pull my sword and stride out the door; my little ones tug my clothes and cry.

sentences.zh: 它家但願富貴，賤妾與君共餔糜。

translations.literal: Other families only wish for wealth and rank; your humble wife will share thin gruel with you.
translations.idiomatic: Others crave riches and rank; I, your lowly wife, will share porridge with you still.

translations.literal: Section Two
translations.idiomatic: Second section

sentences.zh: 共鋪糜，上用倉浪天故，下為黃口小兒。

translations.literal: Together we cook the gruel—above for the blue heaven's sake, below for our yellow-mouthed little children.
translations.idiomatic: We boil the porridge together—for the vast sky above, for our small children below.

sentences.zh: 今時清廉，難犯教言，君復自愛莫為非。

translations.literal: In these times honesty is prized; hard to break the teaching's word—love yourself and do no wrong.
translations.idiomatic: These days are upright; the teaching is hard to violate—take care of yourself and do no evil.

translations.literal: Section Three
translations.idiomatic: Third section

sentences.zh: 今時清廉，難犯教言，君復自愛莫為非。

translations.literal: In these times honesty is prized; hard to break the teaching's word—love yourself and do no wrong.
translations.idiomatic: These times are upright; the teaching is hard to violate—guard yourself and do no wrong.

translations.literal: Go!
translations.idiomatic: Go!

sentences.zh: 吾去為遲，平慎行，望吾歸。

translations.literal: If I leave it will be late—go carefully; look for my return.
translations.idiomatic: I go—it may be long; walk in peace and wait for me to come home.

translations.literal: Section Four
translations.idiomatic: Fourth section

translations.literal: "Western Mountain" / "Willow-Breaking Ballad" — text by Emperor Wen of Wei
translations.idiomatic: "Western Mountain" (tune: "Willow-Breaking Ballad") — text by Emperor Wen of Wei

translations.literal: Section Four
translations.idiomatic: Fourth section

sentences.zh: 西山一何高，高高殊無極。

translations.literal: How high is Western Mountain—so high, beyond all limit.
translations.idiomatic: Western Mountain—how high! Higher than any bound.

sentences.zh: 上有兩仙僮，不飲亦不食。

translations.literal: On its heights two immortal youths— they neither drink nor eat.
translations.idiomatic: At the summit two immortal youths who neither drink nor eat.

sentences.zh: 與我一丸藥，光耀有五色。

translations.literal: They give me one pill of medicine, shining with five colors.
translations.idiomatic: They hand me one elixir pill, radiant with five hues.

translations.literal: Section One
translations.idiomatic: First section

sentences.zh: 服藥四五日，身體生羽翼。

translations.literal: After four or five days of taking the drug, wings grow on my body.
translations.idiomatic: Four or five days after taking the medicine, wings sprout on my body.

sentences.zh: 輕舉乘浮雲，倏忽行萬億。

translations.literal: Lightly I rise riding floating clouds; in a flash I travel a hundred million leagues.
translations.idiomatic: I rise lightly on drifting clouds; in an instant I traverse ten thousand leagues.

sentences.zh: 流覽觀四海，芒芒非所識。

translations.literal: Roaming I view the four seas—vast, vast, nothing I recognize.
translations.idiomatic: I wander viewing the four seas—boundless, unfamiliar on every side.

translations.literal: Section Two
translations.idiomatic: Second section

sentences.zh: 彭祖稱七百，悠悠安可原。

translations.literal: Peng Zu claimed seven hundred years—how far can such long ease be traced?
translations.idiomatic: Peng Zu counted seven hundred years—how can such long life be fathomed?

sentences.zh: 老聃適西戎，於今竟不還。

translations.literal: Old Laozi went west to the Rong—down to today he has not returned.
translations.idiomatic: Laozi went west to the barbarians—he has never come back to this day.

sentences.zh: 王喬假虛詞，赤松垂空言。

translations.literal: Wang Qiao's words are false pretense; Chisong's is empty talk.
translations.idiomatic: Wang Qiao's tales are hollow; Master Red Pine's words are idle.

translations.literal: Section Three
translations.idiomatic: Third section

sentences.zh: 達人識真偽，愚夫好妄傳。

translations.literal: The accomplished man knows truth from falsehood; the fool loves wild rumor.
translations.idiomatic: The sage discerns the real from the sham; the fool delights in vain tales.

sentences.zh: 追念往古事，憒憒千萬端。

translations.literal: I recall affairs of ancient days—confused, confused, in ten thousand ways.
translations.idiomatic: I think back on olden times—tangled, tangled, in endless ways.

sentences.zh: 百家多迂怪，聖道我所觀。

translations.literal: A hundred schools are mostly crooked and strange; the sage's Way is what I observe.
translations.idiomatic: The hundred schools are mostly absurd and odd; the sage's Way is what I follow.

translations.literal: Section Four
translations.idiomatic: Fourth section

translations.literal: "Luofu" / "Lustrous Song: Luofu Ballad" — old lyrics
translations.idiomatic: "Luofu" (tune: "Lustrous Song: Luofu Ballad") — traditional lyrics

translations.literal: Section Three
translations.idiomatic: Third section

sentences.zh: 日出東南隅，照我秦氏樓。

translations.literal: The sun rises in the southeast corner, shining on my house of the Qin clan.
translations.idiomatic: The sun comes up in the southeast, lighting the Qin family's tower.

sentences.zh: 秦氏有好女，自名為羅敷。

translations.literal: The Qin house has a fine daughter; she calls herself Luofu.
translations.idiomatic: The Qins have a lovely daughter who names herself Luofu.

sentences.zh: 羅敷喜蠶桑，采桑城南隅。

translations.literal: Luofu loves raising silkworms; she gathers mulberry leaves south of the city.
translations.idiomatic: Luofu delights in silkworm culture; she picks mulberry south of the wall.

sentences.zh: 青絲為籠係，桂枝為籠鉤。

translations.literal: Green silk for the basket's tie, cassia twigs for the basket's hook.
translations.idiomatic: Green silk binds the basket; cassia branches form the hook.

sentences.zh: 頭上倭墮髻，耳中明月珠。

translations.literal: On her head a drooping bun; in her ears pearls like the bright moon.
translations.idiomatic: Her hair is in a soft falling coil; moon-pearl earrings hang at her ears.

sentences.zh: 緗綺為下帬，紫綺為上襦。

translations.literal: Light red silk for her lower skirt, purple silk for her upper robe.
translations.idiomatic: Crimson gauze for her lower skirt, purple silk for her jacket.

sentences.zh: 行者見羅敷，下儋捋髭須。

translations.literal: Wayfarers who see Luofu stop and adjust their beards.
translations.idiomatic: Passersby who see Luofu halt and smooth their whiskers.

sentences.zh: 少年見羅敷，脫帽著帩頭。

translations.literal: Young men who see Luofu doff their caps and put on headcloths.
translations.idiomatic: Youths who see Luofu take off their caps and don kerchiefs.

sentences.zh: 耕者忘其犂，鋤者忘其鋤。

translations.literal: Ploughmen forget their ploughs; hoe-men forget their hoes.
translations.idiomatic: The plowman forgets his plow; the hoer forgets his hoe.

sentences.zh: 來歸相怒怨，但坐觀羅敷。

translations.literal: Returning home they scold one another—only because they stood watching Luofu.
translations.idiomatic: They come home angry at each other—all for stopping to stare at Luofu.

translations.literal: Section One
translations.idiomatic: First section

sentences.zh: 使君從南來，五馬立躊躇。

translations.literal: The governor comes from the south; five horses stand hesitating.
translations.idiomatic: The magistrate arrives from the south; his five-horse carriage waits undecided.

sentences.zh: 使君遣吏往，問是誰家姝？

translations.literal: The governor sends an officer to ask: whose daughter is this beauty?
translations.idiomatic: The magistrate sends a clerk to inquire whose lovely daughter she is.

sentences.zh: 秦氏有好女，自名為羅敷。

translations.literal: The Qin house has a fine daughter; she calls herself Luofu.
translations.idiomatic: The Qins have a lovely daughter who names herself Luofu.

translations.literal: Luofu—how many years?
translations.idiomatic: How old is Luofu?

sentences.zh: 二十尚不足，十五頗有餘。

translations.literal: Not yet twenty; a bit more than fifteen.
translations.idiomatic: Not quite twenty— a little over fifteen.

sentences.zh: 使君謝羅敷，寧可共載不？

translations.literal: The governor addresses Luofu: will you ride with me?
translations.idiomatic: The magistrate says to Luofu: would you share my carriage?

sentences.zh: 羅敷前置詞，使君一何愚！

translations.literal: Luofu speaks first: how foolish you are, magistrate!
translations.idiomatic: Luofu answers first: magistrate, how foolish you are!

sentences.zh: 使君自有婦，羅敷自有夫。

translations.literal: The magistrate has his own wife; Luofu has her own husband.
translations.idiomatic: You have your own wife, magistrate; I have my own husband.

translations.literal: Section Two
translations.idiomatic: Second section

sentences.zh: 東方千餘騎，夫壻居上頭。

translations.literal: To the east, more than a thousand riders—my husband rides at the head.
translations.idiomatic: Eastward ride more than a thousand horsemen—my husband leads them.

translations.literal: How would you know my husband?
translations.idiomatic: How could you recognize my husband?

translations.literal: A white horse followed by piebald colts.
translations.idiomatic: A white horse with dark-maned foals behind.

sentences.zh: 青絲繫馬尾，黃金絡馬頭。

translations.literal: Green silk ties the horse's tail; gold clasps the horse's head.
translations.idiomatic: Green silk binds the tail; gold filigree crowns the head.

sentences.zh: 腰中鹿盧劒，可直千萬餘。

translations.literal: At his waist a deer-horn sword worth more than ten million.
translations.idiomatic: At his belt a deer-antler sword worth ten million and more.

sentences.zh: 十五府小史，二十朝大夫，三十侍中郎，四十專城居。

translations.literal: At fifteen a petty clerk in the prefecture; at twenty a court grandee; at thirty a palace attendant; at forty he holds a walled city.
translations.idiomatic: At fifteen he served as a minor clerk; at twenty he became a court officer; at thirty an attendant in the palace; at forty he governed a city in his own right.

sentences.zh: 為人潔白晳，鬑鬑頗有須。

translations.literal: Fair-skinned and clean in person; his side whiskers are full.
translations.idiomatic: Fair and bright of countenance; his temple whiskers are ample.

sentences.zh: 盈盈公府步，冉冉府中趨。

translations.literal: With measured steps he paces the offices; slowly he hurries through the halls.
translations.idiomatic: With graceful gait he walks the government halls; unhurried, he moves through the offices.

sentences.zh: 坐中數千人，皆言夫壻殊。

translations.literal: Among thousands seated in the hall, all say her husband is extraordinary.
translations.idiomatic: Among thousands in the assembly, all declare her husband remarkable.

translations.literal: Section Three
translations.idiomatic: Third section

translations.literal: Before it there is a lustrous lyric tune; after it there is hurry.
translations.idiomatic: Before comes a lustrous lyric; after comes the hurried closing.

translations.literal: "West Gate" / "West Gate Ballad" — old lyrics
translations.idiomatic: "West Gate" (tune: "West Gate Ballad") — traditional lyrics

translations.literal: Section Six
translations.idiomatic: Sixth section

translations.literal: Out the west gate, walking, I brood on it.
translations.idiomatic: I go out the west gate and walk, turning it over in my mind.

translations.literal: If we make no joy today, when shall we wait?
translations.idiomatic: If we take no pleasure today, when will we ever?

translations.literal: Section One
translations.idiomatic: First section

translations.literal: Husband, make joy—make joy while the time is ripe.
translations.idiomatic: Man, be merry—be merry while the moment lasts.

sentences.zh: 何能坐愁怫鬱，當復來茲。

translations.literal: How can we sit in gloom and sullen grief? Let us come again here.
translations.idiomatic: Why sit brooding in sullen grief? Come back to this again.

translations.literal: Section Two
translations.idiomatic: Second section

translations.literal: Drink rich wine; roast fat ox.
translations.idiomatic: Drink fine wine; grill a fat ox.

sentences.zh: 請呼心所歡，可用解愁憂。

translations.literal: Call those the heart delights in—they can dispel sorrow and care.
translations.idiomatic: Summon those your heart loves—they can loosen grief and worry.

translations.literal: Section Three
translations.idiomatic: Third section

sentences.zh: 人生不滿百，常懷千歲憂。

translations.literal: Human life does not fill a hundred years, yet we often harbor thousand-year cares.
translations.idiomatic: Life does not reach a hundred, yet we carry worries of a thousand years.

sentences.zh: 晝短而夜長，何不秉燭遊。

translations.literal: Day is short and night is long—why not take up candles and roam?
translations.idiomatic: The day is short, the night is long—why not hold candles and go wandering?

translations.literal: Section Four
translations.idiomatic: Fourth section

sentences.zh: 自‖非‖仙‖人‖王‖子‖喬‖，計‖會‖壽‖命‖難‖‖與‖期‖。

translations.literal: Unless you are the immortal Wang Ziqiao, how can you reckon and match your allotted span of life?
translations.idiomatic: Unless you are the immortal Prince Ziqiao, you cannot count on matching your appointed span of life.

translations.literal: Section Five
translations.idiomatic: Fifth section

sentences.zh: 人壽非金石，年命安可期；

translations.literal: Human life is not metal or stone; how can years and fate be foreknown?
translations.idiomatic: Life is not bronze or stone; how can length of days be predicted?

sentences.zh: 貪財愛惜費，但為後世嗤。

translations.literal: Greedy for wealth, stingy with spending—only for later ages to mock.
translations.idiomatic: Hoarding riches and grudging expense—you will be laughed at by posterity.

translations.literal: Section Six
translations.idiomatic: Sixth section
(End.)

sentences.zh: 一本「燭遊」後「行去之，如雲除，弊車羸馬為自推」，無「自非」以下四十八字。

translations.literal: One edition reads after "candle roam": "Departing, like clouds cleared away, a broken cart and weary horse push themselves on," and lacks the forty-eight characters from "Unless you are the immortal" onward.
translations.idiomatic: One manuscript version, after "roam by candle," adds "Go away like clouds dispersing, a broken cart and exhausted horse forcing themselves onward," and omits the forty-eight characters beginning with "Unless you are the immortal."

translations.literal: "Silent Silent" / "Willow-Breaking Ballad" — old lyrics
translations.idiomatic: "Silent Silent" (tune: "Willow-Breaking Ballad") — traditional lyrics

translations.literal: Section Four
translations.idiomatic: Fourth section

sentences.zh: 默默施行違，厥罰隨事來，末喜殺龍逢，桀放於鳴條。

translations.literal: Silently carrying out what is forbidden—punishment follows the deed; at the end Jie was glad to kill Long Feng, and Jie exiled Tang at Mingtiao.
translations.idiomatic: Quietly doing what is taboo—punishment tracks the act; Jie at last killed Long Feng, and Tang was sent away at Mingtiao.

translations.literal: Section One
translations.idiomatic: First section

sentences.zh: 祖伊言不用，紂頭縣白旄。

translations.literal: Zuyi spoke but was not heeded; Zhou's head was hung on a white banner.
translations.idiomatic: Zuyi's counsel went unheeded; Zhou's head was displayed on a white standard.

sentences.zh: 指鹿用為馬，胡亥以喪軀。

translations.literal: A deer was pointed to and called a horse; Huhai thereby lost his life.
translations.idiomatic: A deer was shown and named a horse; Huhai thus lost his life.

translations.literal: Section Two
translations.idiomatic: Second section

sentences.zh: 夫差臨命絕，乃云負子胥。

translations.literal: Fuchai at life's end still said he had failed Zixu.
translations.idiomatic: Fuchai at the point of death still said he had wronged Zixu.

sentences.zh: 戎王納女樂，以亡其由余。

translations.literal: The Rong king took in women's music and thereby lost his Youyu.
translations.idiomatic: The king of Rong accepted female entertainers and lost Youyu.

sentences.zh: 璧馬禍及虢，二國俱為墟。

translations.literal: The jade and horses brought disaster to Guo—both states became ruins.
translations.idiomatic: The jade and horses ruined Guo—both states turned to wasteland.

translations.literal: Section Three
translations.idiomatic: Third section

sentences.zh: 三夫成市虎，慈母投杼趨。

translations.literal: Three men make a tiger in the market; the fond mother runs to cast away her shuttle.
translations.idiomatic: Three men crying tiger in the market; the loving mother rushes to throw down her loom.

sentences.zh: 卞和之刖足，接予歸草廬。

translations.literal: Bian He's feet cut off; Jieyu returned to his thatched hut.
translations.idiomatic: Bian He had his feet amputated; Jieyu went back to his grass hut.

translations.literal: Section Four
translations.idiomatic: Fourth section

sentences.zh: 《園桃》 《煌煌京洛行》 文帝詞

translations.literal: "Garden Peach" / "Splendid Capital Luoyang Ballad" — text by Emperor Wen of Wei
translations.idiomatic: "Garden Peach" (tune: "Splendid Capital Luoyang Ballad") — text by Emperor Wen of Wei

translations.literal: Section Five
translations.idiomatic: Fifth section

translations.literal: Lush, lush garden peaches—without fruit they grow empty and long.
translations.idiomatic: Flourishing garden peaches—barren, they lengthen in vain.

translations.literal: Empty beauty is hard to feign; a lopsided wheel cannot roll.
translations.idiomatic: Hollow praise is hard to fake; a warped wheel cannot run true.

translations.literal: Section One
translations.idiomatic: First section

translations.literal: Huaiyin suffered the five punishments—when the bird is gone, the bow is stored.
translations.idiomatic: Huaiyin bore the five penalties—when the bird is taken, the bow is put away.

translations.literal: Preserving body and full name—only Zifang alone.
translations.idiomatic: To keep body and reputation intact—only Zifang did so.

translations.literal: Great rage unrestrained; wide robes without belt;
translations.idiomatic: Vast anger uncontrolled; loose robes without a sash;

translations.literal: Much talk, little sincerity—only makes affairs fail.
translations.idiomatic: Many words, little truth—nothing but failure.

translations.literal: Section Two
translations.idiomatic: Second section

translations.literal: Su Qin's persuasions—the six states perished thereby.
translations.idiomatic: Su Qin's doctrines—the six states fell because of them.

translations.literal: Leaning and selling out his lord—being torn by chariots was fitting.
translations.idiomatic: Tilting and betraying his master—quartering by chariots was his due.

sentences.zh: 賢矣陳軫，忠而有謀，楚懷不從，禍卒不救。

translations.literal: Worthy was Chen Zhen—loyal and full of plans; King Huai of Chu did not follow, and disaster came with no rescue.
translations.idiomatic: Chen Zhen was admirable—loyal and scheming; Chu Huai would not listen, and ruin came beyond saving.

translations.literal: Section Three
translations.idiomatic: Third section

sentences.zh: 禍夫吳起，智小謀大，西河何健，伏屍何劣。

translations.literal: Woe for Wu Qi—small wit, grand schemes; how strong at Xihe, how wretched lying dead.
translations.idiomatic: Alas for Wu Qi—clever in small things, bold in large; how vigorous at Xihe, how lowly in death.

translations.literal: Section Four
translations.idiomatic: Fourth section

sentences.zh: 嗟彼郭生，古之雅人，智矣燕昭，可謂得臣。

translations.literal: Ah, that Guo Sheng—an elegant man of old; wise was King Zhao of Yan, one may say he gained a true minister.
translations.idiomatic: Ah, Guo Sheng—the refined man of antiquity; how wise Yan Zhao was—he truly won a minister.

translations.literal: Lofty, lofty Zhonglian—Qi state's lofty scholar;
translations.idiomatic: Towering Zhonglian—Qi's exalted knight;

translations.literal: Northward he refused a thousand in gold; eastward he trod the blue sea.
translations.idiomatic: He declined a thousand gold in the north; he walked the eastern sea.

translations.literal: Section Five
translations.idiomatic: Fifth section

translations.literal: "White Swan" / "Lustrous Song: A Chang"
translations.idiomatic: "White Swan" (tune: "Lustrous Song: A Chang")

translations.literal: 〈Also titled "Flying Swan Ballad"〉
translations.idiomatic: (Also titled "Flying Swan Ballad")

translations.literal: Old lyrics
translations.idiomatic: Traditional lyrics

translations.literal: Section Four
translations.idiomatic: Fourth section

sentences.zh: 飛來雙白鵠，乃從西北來。

translations.literal: A pair of white swans fly in—from the northwest they come.
translations.idiomatic: Two white swans fly in—from the northwest they arrive.

translations.literal: Ten and five, ten and five—they range in rows.
translations.idiomatic: In fives and tens they line up in ranks.

translations.literal: Section One
translations.idiomatic: First section

translations.literal: The wife suddenly falls ill; on the road she cannot keep pace.
translations.idiomatic: His mate falls suddenly ill; on the journey she cannot follow.

sentences.zh: 五里一反顧，六里一裴回。

translations.literal: Every five li he turns his head; every six li he circles back.
translations.idiomatic: Every five leagues he looks back; every six he turns in circles.

translations.literal: Section Two
translations.idiomatic: Second section

sentences.zh: 吾欲銜汝去，口噤不能開；

translations.literal: I would hold you in my beak and go—my mouth is stiff and cannot open;
translations.idiomatic: I want to carry you in my bill and fly—my beak is sealed and will not open;

sentences.zh: 吾欲負汝去，毛羽何摧穨。

translations.literal: I would bear you on my back and go—how broken and drooping are my feathers.
translations.idiomatic: I want to bear you on my back—how tattered and drooping my wings are.

translations.literal: Section Three
translations.idiomatic: Third section

sentences.zh: 樂哉新相知，憂來生別離。

translations.literal: Happy, happy in new acquaintance—grief comes with parting in life.
translations.idiomatic: Joy in new love—sorrow born of parting in this life.

sentences.zh: 躇躊顧羣侶，淚下不自知。

translations.literal: Hesitating, I look back at the flock; tears fall—I know not why.
translations.idiomatic: I linger, glancing at my companions; tears fall unawares.

translations.literal: Section Four
translations.idiomatic: Fourth section

sentences.zh: 念與君離別，氣結不能言。

translations.literal: Thinking that I part from you, my breath knots and I cannot speak.
translations.idiomatic: When I think of parting from you, my breath chokes and words will not come.

sentences.zh: 各各重自愛，道遠歸還難。

translations.literal: Each of you must cherish yourselves well; the road is far and returning is hard.
translations.idiomatic: Each of you, take good care of yourselves—the journey is long, and coming home will be hard.

sentences.zh: 妾當守空房，閉門下重關。

translations.literal: I shall keep to the empty chamber, shut the door and drop the heavy bar.
translations.idiomatic: I will guard the empty room alone, close the door, and bolt it fast.

sentences.zh: 若生當相見，亡者會黃泉。

translations.literal: If we live we shall meet again; if dead we shall meet in the Yellow Springs.
translations.idiomatic: If we live, we shall see each other again; if not, we shall meet in the Yellow Springs.

sentences.zh: 今日樂相樂，延年萬歲期。

translations.literal: Today let us rejoice together in joy—a term of ten thousand years of extended life.
translations.idiomatic: Let us delight in each other today—may our joy last ten thousand years.

translations.literal: From 'Thinking that I part' below is the quickened refrain; before it is the prelude.
translations.idiomatic: The section from 'Thinking that I part' onward is the hurrying refrain; the prelude comes before it.

sentences.zh: 《碣石》 《步出夏門行》 武帝詞

translations.literal: Jieshi / Walking Out the Xia Gate—lyrics by Emperor Wu.
translations.idiomatic: Jieshi (Walking Out the Xia Gate)—words by Emperor Wu of Wei.

translations.literal: Section Four
translations.idiomatic: Fourth section

sentences.zh: 雲行雨步，超越九江之臯，臨觀異同。

translations.literal: Clouds move, rain steps; crossing beyond the marshes of the Nine Rivers, looking down on differences and sameness.
translations.idiomatic: Clouds drift and rain falls; I pass beyond the Nine Rivers' shallows and gaze on all that differs and all that is the same.

sentences.zh: 心意懷游豫，不知當復何從。

translations.literal: In heart and intent I harbor wandering ease; I do not know where I should go again.
translations.idiomatic: My heart is full of roaming pleasure, yet I no longer know which way to turn.

sentences.zh: 經過至我碣石，心惆悵我東海。

translations.literal: Passing by to my Jieshi stone, my heart is melancholy for my Eastern Sea.
translations.idiomatic: I come to my Jieshi stone, and my heart aches for the Eastern Sea.

translations.literal: From 'Clouds move' to here is the prelude.
translations.idiomatic: From 'Clouds move' through here is the prelude (yan).

translations.literal: East I ascend Jieshi stone to gaze at the vast sea.
translations.idiomatic: I climb Jieshi stone in the east to look upon the vast sea.

translations.literal: How gently the waters; the mountain isle rises steep and tall.
translations.idiomatic: The waters stretch vast and calm; the island peaks rise sharp and tall.

translations.literal: Trees grow in clusters; every hundred grasses lush and thick.
translations.idiomatic: Trees crowd in thickets; every kind of grass flourishes green.

translations.literal: Autumn wind sighs bleak; great surges boil up.
translations.idiomatic: The autumn wind sighs cold; mighty waves surge and swell.

translations.literal: The sun and moon's course—as if issuing from within it;
translations.idiomatic: The sun and moon run their course as if born from its heart;

translations.literal: The starry river brilliant—as if issuing from inside it.
translations.idiomatic: the Milky Way blazes bright as if poured from its depths.

translations.literal: How exceedingly fortunate!
translations.idiomatic: How very fortunate indeed!

translations.literal: A song to declare my intent.
translations.idiomatic: I sing this song to speak my mind.

translations.literal: Gazing at the Vast Sea.
translations.idiomatic: Gazing at the Vast Sea.

translations.literal: Section One
translations.idiomatic: First section

translations.literal: In the tenth month of early winter, the north wind eddies and swirls.
translations.idiomatic: In the tenth month of early winter, the north wind whirls and turns.

translations.literal: The weather is stern and clear; heavy frost falls fine and dense.
translations.idiomatic: The sky is hard and clear; thick frost falls in fine flakes.

sentences.zh: 鵾雞晨鳴，鴻鴈南飛，鷙鳥潛藏，熊羆窟棲。

translations.literal: At dawn the pheasant-cock cries; wild geese fly south; fierce birds hide in concealment; bears and black bears den and roost.
translations.idiomatic: At dawn the golden pheasant calls; wild geese wing south; birds of prey lie hidden; bears and grizzlies hole up in their dens.

translations.literal: Plowshares and hoes are laid aside; harvests piled in the threshing yards.
translations.idiomatic: Plowshares and hoes are stilled; grain is heaped in the threshing yards.

translations.literal: Inns are properly established to open passage for merchants.
translations.idiomatic: Roadside inns stand ready to let traveling merchants pass.

translations.literal: How exceedingly fortunate!
translations.idiomatic: How very fortunate indeed!

translations.literal: A song to chant my intent.
translations.idiomatic: I sing this song to voice my purpose.

translations.literal: Tenth Month of Winter.
translations.idiomatic: The Tenth Month of Winter.

translations.literal: Section Two
translations.idiomatic: Second section

translations.literal: Local soils differ; north of the river the cold is severe.
translations.idiomatic: Each land has its own ways; north of the Yellow River the cold runs deep.

translations.literal: Floating ice drifts; boats and ships find travel hard.
translations.idiomatic: Ice floes drift and spin; boats can hardly make way.

translations.literal: An awl will not enter the ground; thick reeds hide deep recesses.
translations.idiomatic: You cannot drive a awl into the earth; tall rushes bury deep hollows.

translations.literal: Waters dry up and do not flow; ice is hard enough to tread upon.
translations.idiomatic: Streams fail and cease to run; the ice is firm enough to walk on.

translations.literal: Scholars in hiding are poor; bold knights-errant lightly scorn others.
translations.idiomatic: Recluses and scholars live in want; swaggering bravoes treat wrongdoing lightly.

translations.literal: The heart constantly sighs in resentment; sorrowful and anxious, much grief.
translations.idiomatic: The heart forever murmurs with grievance; anxious thoughts bring endless sorrow.

translations.literal: How exceedingly fortunate!
translations.idiomatic: How very fortunate indeed!

translations.literal: A song to chant my intent.
translations.idiomatic: I sing this song to voice my purpose.

translations.literal: Cold North of the River.
translations.idiomatic: Cold North of the River.

translations.literal: Section Three
translations.idiomatic: Third section

translations.literal: The divine tortoise may live long, yet still has its end;
translations.idiomatic: Though the sacred tortoise lives long, it too must reach its end;

translations.literal: The soaring serpent rides mist, yet in the end becomes dust and ash.
translations.idiomatic: though the flying serpent rides the mist, it ends as dust and ash.

translations.literal: An old steed lies in the stable, yet its will is for a thousand li;
translations.idiomatic: An aged thoroughbred may rest in the stall, yet its ambition is still a thousand li;

translations.literal: A man of fierce resolve in his twilight years—his strong heart does not cease.
translations.idiomatic: a hero in his declining years—his mighty heart never stops.

translations.literal: The term of waxing and waning is not only in Heaven;
translations.idiomatic: Fortune's ebb and flow is not Heaven's alone;

translations.literal: The blessing of nurturing ease can obtain everlasting years.
translations.idiomatic: by cultivating peace and contentment one may win long life.

translations.literal: How exceedingly fortunate!
translations.idiomatic: How very fortunate indeed!

translations.literal: A song to chant my intent.
translations.idiomatic: I sing this song to voice my purpose.

translations.literal: Though the Divine Tortoise Lives Long.
translations.idiomatic: Though the Divine Tortoise Lives Long.

translations.literal: Section Four
translations.idiomatic: Fourth section

translations.literal: Have I Ever / Splendid Song: Have I Ever—ancient lyrics.
translations.idiomatic: Have I Ever (Splendid Song: Have I Ever)—ancient text.

translations.literal: Section Five
translations.idiomatic: Fifth section

translations.literal: When have I ever been quick to rejoice alone without care?
translations.idiomatic: When was I ever swift to delight alone and free of worry?

translations.literal: One need only drink rich wine and broil fat oxen.
translations.idiomatic: All one need do is drink fine wine and roast fat beef.

translations.literal: Section One
translations.idiomatic: First section

sentences.zh: 長兄為二千石，中兄被貂裘。

translations.literal: The elder brother holds two-thousand-dan rank; the middle brother wears sable fur.
translations.idiomatic: My eldest brother holds office at two thousand dan; my middle brother wraps himself in sable.

translations.literal: Section Two
translations.idiomatic: Second section

sentences.zh: 小弟雖無官爵，鞍馬{馬反}{馬反}，往來王侯長者遊。

translations.literal: The younger brother though without rank or fief—saddle and horse prancing, prancing—comes and goes among kings, marquises, and elder worthies.
translations.idiomatic: Though I, the youngest, hold no title or stipend, my horse prances at the saddle as I ride among lords and great men.

translations.literal: Section Three
translations.idiomatic: Third section

sentences.zh: 但當在王侯殿上，快獨摴蒲六博，對坐彈碁。

translations.literal: One need only be in the halls of kings and marquises—swift to rejoice alone at chu-pu and liu-bo, facing each other playing go.
translations.idiomatic: Let me only sit in princes' halls—happy alone casting dice and playing six-board, facing a partner over the go board.

translations.literal: Section Four
translations.idiomatic: Fourth section

translations.literal: A man living in the world—each should exert himself;
translations.idiomatic: A man in this world must each do his utmost;

translations.literal: Hurried—dusk presses near; scarcely any time to remain.
translations.idiomatic: time presses toward evening; little stays before us.

translations.literal: Section Five
translations.idiomatic: Fifth section

sentences.zh: 少小相觸抵，寒苦常相隨，忿恚安足諍，吾中道與卿共別離。

translations.literal: From youth we jostled and clashed; cold and hardship always followed together—what use wrangling in anger and resentment? Midway on the road I part from you.
translations.idiomatic: Since we were boys we have rubbed each other raw; cold and want dogged us—why quarrel in rage? Halfway on life's road I must leave you.

sentences.zh: 約身奉事君，禮節不可虧。

translations.literal: I constrain my person to serve you; ritual and propriety must not be diminished.
translations.idiomatic: I bind myself to serve you; courtesy and rites must never be broken.

sentences.zh: 上慙滄浪之夫，下顧黃口小兒。

translations.literal: Above I shame the man of the Canglang; below I look to the yellow-mouthed little children.
translations.idiomatic: Above, I am shamed before the fisherman of the Canglang; below, I must care for my young children at the breast.

sentences.zh: 奈何復老心皇皇，獨悲誰能知！

translations.literal: Alas—again in old age my heart is restless and anxious; who can know this grief alone!
translations.idiomatic: Yet in old age my heart only grows more restless—this sorrow, who can understand?

translations.literal: From 'From youth' below is the quickened refrain; before it is the prelude.
translations.idiomatic: From 'From youth' onward is the hurrying refrain; the prelude comes before it.

translations.literal: Setting Wine / Wild Field Yellow Sparrow Song
translations.idiomatic: Setting Wine (Wild Field Yellow Sparrow Song)

translations.literal: The Konghou Prelude also uses this tune.
translations.idiomatic: The Konghou Prelude also uses this melody.

translations.literal: Lyrics by the Prince of Dong'e
translations.idiomatic: Words by the Prince of Dong'e (Cao Zhi)

translations.literal: Section Four
translations.idiomatic: Fourth section

sentences.zh: 置酒高殿上，親交從我游。

translations.literal: Wine is set in the high hall; kin and friends follow me in roaming.
translations.idiomatic: Wine is laid out in the lofty hall; kin and friends roam with me.

sentences.zh: 中廚辦豊膳，烹羊宰肥牛。

translations.literal: The middle kitchen prepares rich fare—boiling sheep and slaughtering fat oxen.
translations.idiomatic: The inner kitchen serves lavish dishes—boiling sheep and butchering fat cattle.

sentences.zh: 秦箏何忼慨，齊瑟和且柔。

translations.literal: How boldly stirring the Qin zither; the Qi se harmonious and soft.
translations.idiomatic: The Qin zither sounds bold and stirring; the Qi se answers soft and gentle.

translations.literal: Section One
translations.idiomatic: First section

sentences.zh: 陽阿奏奇舞，京洛出名謳。

translations.literal: At Yang'e they perform wondrous dance; from the capital come famed songs.
translations.idiomatic: At Yang'e they dance marvels; from Luoyang come songs of renown.

sentences.zh: 樂飲過三爵，緩帶傾庶羞，主稱千金壽，賓奉萬年酬。

translations.literal: Joyfully drinking past three cups, loosening the belt to pour out many delicacies—the host speaks of a thousand in gold for long life; the guest offers ten thousand years in return.
translations.idiomatic: We drink past three rounds in delight, belts loosened, dishes poured forth—the host toasts a thousand pieces of gold for long life; the guest returns a wish for ten thousand years.

translations.literal: Section Two
translations.idiomatic: Second section

sentences.zh: 久要不可忘，薄終義所尤。

translations.literal: Long-standing promises must not be forgotten; a shabby ending is what righteousness most reproaches.
translations.idiomatic: Old pledges must never be forgotten; to fail at the end is what honor condemns most.

sentences.zh: 謙謙君子德，磬折欲何求。

translations.literal: The modest, modest gentleman's virtue—bowing like a stone chime, what does he seek?
translations.idiomatic: The humble gentleman's virtue—bowed like a sounding stone, what more does he want?

sentences.zh: 盛時不再來，百年忽我遒。

translations.literal: The flourishing age does not come again; a hundred years suddenly hurries me on.
translations.idiomatic: The golden season never returns; a hundred years rush past in a blink.

translations.literal: Section Three
translations.idiomatic: Third section

sentences.zh: 驚風飄白日，光景馳西流。

translations.literal: Startled wind blows the white sun; light and shadow gallop westward.
translations.idiomatic: A sudden wind scatters the bright sun; light and shadow race toward the west.

sentences.zh: 生存華屋處，零落歸山丘。

translations.literal: Living one dwells in splendid houses; fallen and scattered one returns to the hillock.
translations.idiomatic: Alive we live in painted halls; stripped away, we go back to the hillock.

sentences.zh: 先民誰不死，知命復何憂！

translations.literal: Which of the ancients did not die? Knowing fate—what further grief!
translations.idiomatic: Who among the ancients did not die? Once fate is known, what is left to grieve?

translations.literal: Section Four
translations.idiomatic: Fourth section

translations.literal: For Joy / Full Song
translations.idiomatic: For Joy (Full Song Ballad)

translations.literal: Section Four
translations.idiomatic: Fourth section

sentences.zh: 為樂未幾時，遭世險巇，逢此百離；

translations.literal: Joy had not lasted long when I met a perilous age and encountered these hundred partings;
translations.idiomatic: Hardly had joy begun when the age turned treacherous and a hundred separations fell upon me;

translations.literal: Orphaned and poisoned, sorrow and vexation hard to sustain.
translations.idiomatic: alone and afflicted, grief and anguish I can barely bear.

translations.literal: Gazing far at the pole star—the sky brightens, the moon shifts.
translations.idiomatic: I stare toward the pole star—dawn breaks and the moon moves on.

translations.literal: When sorrow comes it fills the heart—who will know me?
translations.idiomatic: Sorrow floods my heart—who will understand?

translations.literal: Section One
translations.idiomatic: First section

translations.literal: Sorrowful and anxious, much thought and consideration; bright and unsettled, not at peace.
translations.idiomatic: Anxious thoughts crowd my mind; I lie awake, unable to rest.

sentences.zh: 禍福無形，唯念古人，遜位躬耕。

translations.literal: Fortune and disaster have no fixed form; I think only of the ancients who yielded the throne and plowed with their own hands.
translations.idiomatic: Weal and woe have no shape; I think of the ancients who abdicated and farmed for themselves.

translations.literal: Thus my wish is fulfilled; by this I quiet myself.
translations.idiomatic: In this my wish is granted; by it I find peace.

translations.literal: I myself despise mountain dwelling; guarding this one glory.
translations.idiomatic: I scorn life on the mountain peaks; I hold to this single honor.

translations.literal: Section Two
translations.idiomatic: Second section

translations.literal: Do not—autumn's biting wind rises.
translations.idiomatic: When autumn's sharp wind rises—

translations.literal: West I tread the vast sea; my heart cannot be at peace.
translations.idiomatic: I wander west toward the vast sea, and my heart cannot rest.

translations.literal: I gather my robe and rise to gaze into the night; the Dipper stands athwart.
translations.idiomatic: I wrap my robe and rise to watch the night—the Big Dipper spans the sky.

translations.literal: The starry river shines on me; going, going—I have no other course.
translations.idiomatic: The Milky Way lights my way; I go on—there is nothing else for me.

translations.literal: Serving the two parents—weariness of heart can be told.
translations.idiomatic: To serve both my parents—how much my heart has labored, words can barely tell.

translations.literal: Section Three
translations.idiomatic: Third section

sentences.zh: 窮達天所為，智者不愁，多為少憂。

translations.literal: Poor or eminent—Heaven ordains it; the wise man does not grieve, the many grieve for the few.
translations.idiomatic: Fortune and failure are Heaven's doing; the wise do not brood, though the many fret over little.

translations.literal: At ease in poverty, delighting in the upright Way—take Master Zhuang as teacher.
translations.idiomatic: Content in poverty, joy in the true Way—I take Zhuang Zhou as my master.

translations.literal: Those who leave behind their names are honored; Zixi shares the peril.
translations.idiomatic: Men who renounce fame are noble; Zixi walked the same hard road.

translations.literal: The two worthies of old—their names hang for a thousand autumns.
translations.idiomatic: Those two sages of antiquity—their names endure a thousand years.

translations.literal: Section Four
translations.idiomatic: Fourth section

translations.literal: Drink wine and sing and dance—if not joyous, what need is there!
translations.idiomatic: Drink, sing, and dance—if you will not rejoice, what is the point!

sentences.zh: 善哉照觀日月，日月馳驅。

translations.literal: How good it is to gaze upon the sun and moon—the sun and moon gallop and drive.
translations.idiomatic: How fine to watch the sun and moon race their course across the sky!

translations.literal: Bumpy and jolting in the world—what is there, what is not!
translations.idiomatic: Life in this world is rough and uneven—what do we truly have or lack!

translations.literal: Greedy for wealth and stingy with spending—how foolish this is!
translations.idiomatic: To hoard money and grudge every expense—how utterly foolish!

sentences.zh: 命如鑿石見火，居世竟能幾時？

translations.literal: Life is like striking stone to see fire—how many seasons can one dwell in the world?
translations.idiomatic: Life is like flint struck for a spark—how long can anyone stay in this world?

sentences.zh: 但當歡樂自娛，盡心極所熙怡。

translations.literal: One need only rejoice and amuse oneself— exhaust the heart in utmost gladness and ease.
translations.idiomatic: Only rejoice and amuse yourself—give your heart fully to every delight.

sentences.zh: 安善養君德性，百年保此期頤。

translations.literal: At peace, nurture your lord's moral nature—a hundred years guard this term of old age.
translations.idiomatic: Live at peace, cultivate virtue and character—may you keep this span to a ripe old age.

translations.literal: From 'Drink wine' below is the quickened refrain.
translations.idiomatic: From 'Drink wine' onward is the hurrying refrain.

translations.literal: Summer Gate / Walking Out the Xia Gate
translations.idiomatic: Summer Gate (Walking Out the Xia Gate)

translations.literal: Also titled Longxi Journey
translations.idiomatic: Also known as Longxi Journey

translations.literal: Lyrics by Emperor Ming
translations.idiomatic: Words by Emperor Ming of Wei

translations.literal: Section Two
translations.idiomatic: Second section

translations.literal: Walking out the Xia Gate, east I ascend Mount Shouyang.
translations.idiomatic: I walk out the Xia Gate and climb Mount Shouyang to the east.

translations.literal: Alas, Bo Yi—Confucius called him worthy.
translations.idiomatic: Alas for Bo Yi—Confucius named him a sage.

translations.literal: The gentleman yields and steps back; the petty man scrambles to be first;
translations.idiomatic: The noble man steps aside; the small man fights for the lead;

translations.literal: Only these two men—to this day their names are handed down.
translations.idiomatic: only these two—still praised in song today.

translations.literal: The forest bell receives the farewell; the season shifts, the time turns.
translations.idiomatic: The bell marks the season's turn; the year moves on.

translations.literal: Sun and moon do not stay; who can long endure?
translations.idiomatic: Sun and moon never pause—who can last forever?

translations.literal: How good—again how good; pluck the strings and sing—the feelings rejoice.
translations.idiomatic: How good, how good again—to strum and sing and let the heart rejoice.

translations.literal: Section One
translations.idiomatic: First section

sentences.zh: 商風夕起，悲彼秋蟬，變形易色，隨風東西。

translations.literal: The merchant wind rises at evening; I grieve for the autumn cicadas—changing form and shifting hue, following the wind east and west.
translations.idiomatic: At dusk the trade wind rises; I pity the autumn cicadas—changing color, blown east and west.

sentences.zh: 乃眷西顧，雲霧相連，丹霞蔽日，采虹帶天。

translations.literal: Then I turn my gaze westward—cloud and mist connect; cinnabar clouds hide the sun; rainbow girds the sky.
translations.idiomatic: I look west—cloud and mist merge; red clouds veil the sun; rainbows belt the heavens.

sentences.zh: 弱水潺潺，落葉翩翩，孤禽失羣，悲鳴其間。

translations.literal: The weak waters murmur; fallen leaves flutter; a lone bird loses its flock—mournful cries between them.
translations.idiomatic: Weak waters trickle; leaves drift down; a lone bird lost from the flock wails among them.

sentences.zh: 善哉殊復善，悲鳴在其間。

translations.literal: How good—again how good; mournful cries between them.
translations.idiomatic: How good, how good—the grieving cries between.

translations.literal: Section Two
translations.idiomatic: Second section

translations.literal: Morning I roam the clear cool; at dusk I sigh to return.
translations.idiomatic: In the morning I wander the clear streams; at dusk I sigh to go home.

translations.literal: Above 'Morning I roam' is the prelude.
translations.idiomatic: Before 'Morning I roam' is the prelude (yan).

translations.literal: Hurried—dusk presses near; crows and magpies fly south.
translations.idiomatic: Time presses toward evening; crows and magpies wing south.

translations.literal: Three times around the tree—on which branch can one roost?
translations.idiomatic: Three circuits around the tree—which branch can I rest on?

translations.literal: Suddenly meeting wind and rain—the tree breaks, branches snap.
translations.idiomatic: Suddenly wind and rain strike—the tree splits, boughs shatter.

translations.literal: The male comes and startles the female; the female alone grieves in roosting.
translations.idiomatic: The cock bird arrives and frightens the hen; she broods alone in sorrow.

translations.literal: By night she loses her flock-mates—mournful cries eddy and swirl.
translations.idiomatic: At night she loses her companions—her sad cries circle back.

translations.literal: Luxuriant, luxuriant the thorns and brambles; the kudzu grows thick and long.
translations.idiomatic: Thick thorns and brambles; creeping vines run on and on.

translations.literal: Moved by that wind-borne man, melancholy—I pity myself.
translations.idiomatic: Moved by that wanderer in the wind, I am desolate and grieve for myself.

translations.literal: When the moon is full it wanes; flowers do not bloom again in profusion;
translations.idiomatic: The full moon must wane; glory does not bloom twice;

translations.literal: The saying of old—alas, a single word.
translations.idiomatic: so runs the ancient saying—ah, in a single phrase.

translations.literal: From 'Hurried' below is the quickened refrain.
translations.idiomatic: From 'Hurried' onward is the hurrying refrain.

sentences.zh: 《王者布大化》 《櫂歌行》 明帝詞

translations.literal: The King Spreads Great Transformation / Oar Song—lyrics by Emperor Ming
translations.idiomatic: The King Spreads Great Transformation (Oar Song)—words by Emperor Ming

translations.literal: Section Five
translations.idiomatic: Fifth section

sentences.zh: 王者布大化，配乾稽后祗。

translations.literal: The king spreads great transformation, matching Heaven and examining the sovereign's mandate.
translations.idiomatic: The king spreads his great transforming power, aligning with Heaven and tracing the mandate of the ruler.

sentences.zh: 陽育則陰殺，晷景應度移。

translations.literal: Yang nurtures then yin slays; sundial shadow answers as the degree shifts.
translations.idiomatic: Where yang gives life, yin takes it; the gnomon's shadow moves with the seasons.

translations.literal: Section One
translations.idiomatic: First section

sentences.zh: 文德以時振，武功伐不隨。

translations.literal: Civil virtue is raised in season; martial achievement strikes where none can follow.
translations.idiomatic: Culture is roused at the proper time; military might falls where none resist.

sentences.zh: 重華儛干戚，有苗服從媯。

translations.literal: Emperor Shun danced with shield and axe; the Miao people submitted to Yu.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Shun danced with shield and axe until the Miao people bowed to Yu.

translations.literal: Section Two
translations.idiomatic: Second section

sentences.zh: 蠢爾吳蜀虜，馮江棲山阻。

translations.literal: Stupid you Wu and Shu captives—perching by the river, dwelling in mountain barriers.
translations.idiomatic: Foolish foes of Wu and Shu—nested by the Yangzi, hiding in mountain passes.

sentences.zh: 哀哀王士民，瞻仰靡依怙。

translations.literal: Alas, alas the king's knights and people—gazing up, none to rely on or shelter them.
translations.idiomatic: Alas for the king's soldiers and folk—looking up, they have none to lean on.

translations.literal: Section Three
translations.idiomatic: Third section

sentences.zh: 皇上悼愍斯，宿昔奮天怒。

translations.literal: The emperor grieves and pities this; from of old he roused Heaven's wrath.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor mourns and pities them; long ago he stirred Heaven's anger.

sentences.zh: 發我許昌宮，列舟于長浦。

translations.literal: He set out from my Xuchang palace, arraying boats on the long shore.
translations.idiomatic: He marched from Xuchang palace and lined ships along the long embankment.

translations.literal: Section Four
translations.idiomatic: Fourth section

sentences.zh: 翌日乘波揚，棹歌悲且涼。

translations.literal: Next day riding the waves he raised sail—the oar song mournful and cool.
translations.idiomatic: The next day he rode the waves; the oar song was bleak and cold.

sentences.zh: 太常拂白日，旗幟紛設張。

translations.literal: The Grand Steward brushed aside the white sun; banners and flags were set out in profusion.
translations.idiomatic: The chamberlain cleared the white sun; flags and pennants fluttered in rows.

translations.literal: Section Five
translations.idiomatic: Fifth section

sentences.zh: 將抗旄與鉞，燿威於彼方。

translations.literal: He will raise battle-flags and axes, blazing might in that land.
translations.idiomatic: He will lift standards and battle-axes and show his power in that realm.

sentences.zh: 伐辠以弔民，清我東南疆。

translations.literal: Punishing guilt to comfort the people—clearing my eastern and southern borders.
translations.idiomatic: He punishes the guilty to comfort the people and clears our eastern and southern frontiers.

translations.literal: From 'He will raise' below is the quickened refrain.
translations.idiomatic: From 'He will raise' onward is the hurrying refrain.

sentences.zh: 《洛陽行》 《鴈門太守行》 古詞

translations.literal: Luoyang Journey / Wild Goose Gate Magistrate Song—ancient lyrics
translations.idiomatic: Luoyang Journey (Wild Goose Gate Magistrate Song)—ancient text

translations.literal: Section Eight
translations.idiomatic: Eighth section

sentences.zh: 孝和帝在時，洛陽令王君，本自益州廣漢民，小行宦，學通五經論。

translations.literal: When Emperor Xiaohe was on the throne, Magistrate Wang Jun of Luoyang—originally a commoner of Guanghan in Yizhou—entered minor service, studied and mastered the Five Classics and their commentaries.
translations.idiomatic: Under Emperor Xiaohe, Luoyang magistrate Wang Jun came from Guanghan in Yizhou; as a young man he entered service and mastered the Five Classics and their glosses.

translations.literal: Section One
translations.idiomatic: First section

translations.literal: Clearly knowing laws and ordinances—official caps and belts through generations.
translations.idiomatic: He knew the laws thoroughly—his family had worn official rank for generations.

sentences.zh: 從溫補洛陽令，治行致賢，{扌雝}護百姓，子養萬民。

translations.literal: From Wen he was transferred to supplement Luoyang magistrate; his governance reached excellence—protecting the hundred surnames, nurturing the myriad people as his children.
translations.idiomatic: Promoted from Wen to Luoyang magistrate, he governed with such excellence that he sheltered the common people and raised the myriad folk as his own children.

translations.literal: Section Two
translations.idiomatic: Second section

translations.literal: Outwardly he practiced stern government; inwardly he harbored compassionate kindness.
translations.idiomatic: Outwardly stern, inwardly full of humane care.

sentences.zh: 文武備具，料民富貧，移惡子姓名，五篇著里端。

translations.literal: Complete in civil and martial arts—assessing people's wealth and poverty, moving the names of wicked sons—five registers posted at the lane head.
translations.idiomatic: Skilled in both civil and military affairs, he gauged rich and poor, posted the names of evil youths on five registers at each lane end.

translations.literal: Section Three
translations.idiomatic: Third section

translations.literal: For wounding and killing a person—the whole five-household unit shares guilt, door facing door.
translations.idiomatic: If one committed murder, the whole neighborhood shared punishment, door to door.

sentences.zh: 禁鎦矛八尺，捕輕薄少年，加笞決辠，詣馬市論。

translations.literal: He forbade eight-foot spears, seized frivolous youths, added flogging and fixed guilt, sending them to the horse market for judgment.
translations.idiomatic: He banned long spears, seized rowdy youths, flogged them and sent them to the horse market for sentencing.

translations.literal: Section Four
translations.idiomatic: Fourth section

sentences.zh: 無妄發賦，念在理冤，敕吏正獄，不得苛煩。

translations.literal: He did not levy taxes without cause—his thought was to set right wrongs; he ordered clerks to correct lawsuits and not be harsh or troublesome.
translations.idiomatic: He levied no arbitrary taxes, intent on righting injustice; he told clerks to judge fairly and not harass the people.

translations.literal: For expenses he used thirty coins to buy rope and pole for rites.
translations.idiomatic: For official costs he spent thirty cash on cord and poles for ritual use.

translations.literal: Section Five
translations.idiomatic: Fifth section

translations.literal: Worthy, worthy!
translations.idiomatic: Worthy indeed! Worthy indeed!

translations.literal: In our county—Magistrate Wang Jun.
translations.idiomatic: In our county—Magistrate Wang Jun.

translations.literal: Clerks and officials in caps and belts—serving the emperor.
translations.idiomatic: His clerks in their caps and belts served the emperor faithfully.

translations.literal: Chief clerk and registrar—each man was the right choice.
translations.idiomatic: Recorder and chief clerk—each post had the right man.

translations.literal: Section Six
translations.idiomatic: Sixth section

translations.literal: Holding office in the district, he dared not dispense favors.
